text: Stella Obasanjo (née Abebe; 14 November 1945 – 23 October 2005) served as the First Lady of Nigeria from 1999 until her death. She was the wife of former President Olusegun Obasanjo, though she was not the First Lady in 1976, when Obasanjo was military head of state following the assassination of General Muritala Mohammed. Born in Iruekpen, Esan West, Edo State, she was the daughter of Dr. Christopher Abebe, who was the first indigenous (African) chairman of the United Africa Company (UAC) Nigeria. She began her education at Our Lady of the Apostles Primary School and later attended St. Theresa's College, where she obtained her West African School Certificate in 1964 with grade one and the higher school certificate two years later. She enrolled at the University of Ife (now Obafemi Awolowo University), Ile-Ife, for a bachelor's degree in English from 1967 to 1969, then transferred to the UK in 1970 to study insurance in London and Edinburgh, Scotland, completing her studies by 1974. In 1976, she earned a certificate as confidential secretary from Pitman College and returned to Nigeria. She married General Obasanjo, with whom she had one son, Olumuyiwa Obasanjo, born in 1977. Upon becoming First Lady in 1999 after her husband's election as president, she established the Child Care Trust to support underprivileged and/or disabled children. As First Lady, she joined the Campaign Against Female Genital Mutilation and on 6 February 2003 declared the day the International Day of Zero Tolerance to Female Genital Mutilation. Reporters Without Borders reported that Orobosa Omo-Ojo, publisher of the Lagos-based Nigerian Midwest Herald, was arrested on Stella Obasanjo's orders on 2 May 2005 and taken to Akure prison after an article titled "Greedy Stella" was published the previous week. Obasanjo died at age 59 from complications of cosmetic surgery at a private health clinic in Puerto Banús, Marbella, Spain, on 23 October 2005. The surgeon, identified only as "AM" in court, was sentenced to one year in prison in September 2009 for "causing homicide through negligence," disqualified from medicine for three years, and ordered to pay €120,000 (approximately US$176,000) in compensation to her son. Prosecutors had requested a two-year jail term and five-year disqualification. A request for compensation from the Nigerian government was rejected. The physician had misplaced a tube intended for a liposuction procedure into Obasanjo's abdominal cavity, resulting in a punctured colon and lacerated liver. She died two days after the surgery. The doctor did not answer his mobile phone when called after the procedure and reportedly left her for four hours. It is believed she might have survived had she been hospitalised in time.
